name: Tomas Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I work as a field researcher for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write and maintain the stock software a tech company sells to supermarkets and big shops. It tells a warehouse how many boxes of cereal are on which shelf and when to order more. Most days I'm in the office by nine, I work through bug reports from customers, and I write Java, which is an older programming language, the same way I learned it at university.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work with a clear result: the numbers either add up or they don't. What wears me out is the company chasing every new trend, and now management keeps sending emails about AI tools I've never opened. I'm 27, engaged to Amira, and we're getting married next summer. I've saved well, partly for the wedding and partly for a house, because I want to do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted it out, like it always does. A lot of money chased a fashion and most of it got burned. At work I'd say good developers who know their systems are still worth paying, and I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My job stays the same, my pay stays good, and I don't have to learn something I never wanted. It would also mean I can plan the wedding and the house without a cloud over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep saving, about 900 a month toward the house deposit. After the wedding, Amira and I would buy a small house near both our families, probably in the area where my parents live. I'd stay at my company as long as they treat me fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It would feel like the world coming back to its senses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said near both families. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family is where you get help and give help, not from the government. My mother wants to see grandchildren on Sundays, and Amira's father isn't well. Living ten minutes from both means we can look after them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. House prices are high, but with what I've saved we'd manage. Maybe the company could get sold, but there are plenty of other jobs in the city for someone who knows Java.

say: The **market sorted it out**, as it always does.
Good developers who **know their systems** are still worth paying.
think: I'd be **relieved** to keep my job without learning tools I never wanted.
The **wedding and house** could be planned without a cloud.
do: Keep saving about **900 a month** toward the house deposit.
Buy a **small house** near both families after the wedding.
feel: **Calm**, like the world **coming back** to its senses.
S0.quote: Family is where you get help and give help, not from the government.
fieldNote: Sees the plateau as the **market** correcting a fashion.
His plans run in a **set order**: wedding, then house, then children.
Wants to live near **both families** to care for them.

steps.text: Keep maintaining the warehouse stock software as normal
Save about 900 a month toward the house deposit
Buy a small house near both families after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have every right to use new tools, but they should be honest with their staff about what it means. At work I'd keep quiet mostly. With my friends at the mosque I'd say the young ones should learn a trade as well as a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in trouble. Coding is on the list of things AI takes over, and I've never even opened the tools. If the company wants fewer developers, the one who refuses the new tools goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what management actually does, because they announce a lot and do less. If I saw the team shrinking, I'd look for a job at a slower company, maybe a bank or a public utility that still runs older systems. And I'd hold off on buying the house until the job felt solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be cross with myself for not trying the tools, and cross with the company for forcing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Amira the truth: the house might wait a year, but the wedding goes ahead. My fiancée Amira is a nurse, so her job is steadier than mine in this picture, and my pride wouldn't love that. I'd still say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be cross with yourself for not trying the tools. Would you try them now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if I had to, but slowly and only for small things. I don't like handing my work to something I can't check line by line. I'd rather be slower and know my code is right.

say: Companies may use new tools but must be **honest with staff**.
Young people should learn **a trade** as well as a degree.
think: I'm **in trouble**, because coding is on the list and I've never used the tools.
The one who **refuses the tools** goes first.
do: Wait **a few months** to see what management actually does.
Look for work at a **bank or utility** still running older systems.
Hold off on the **house** until the job feels solid.
feel: **Anxious**, and **cross** with both himself and the company.
S1.quote: My fiancée Amira is a nurse, so her job is steadier than mine in this picture, and my pride wouldn't love that.
fieldNote: Knows that **refusing AI** puts him at the front of the cut line.
Keeps the **wedding** fixed but lets the house slip a year.
His pride is touched by **Amira**, a nurse, becoming the steadier earner.

steps.text: Wait a few months to see management's AI plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech companies rushed this out without a thought for ordinary families, and they should carry the cost. I wouldn't call for handouts, but I'd say these companies owe something. At the mosque, people would be talking about nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is finished, probably within a year. If AI can do almost any thinking work better and cheaper, maintaining stock software is the first thing to go. My savings would hold us for a long time, but a man is supposed to provide, and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the wedding smaller and keep the rest of the money in cash. I'd go to my father's electronics repair shop and ask to learn the trade, because fixing things by hand gives maybe three more years before robots arrive. And Amira and I would live with my parents for a while instead of buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel ashamed, which isn't fair, but that's how it would feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say if you asked to join the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say he always told me so. He wanted me to take over the shop and I chose the computer job. He'd be pleased and sad at the same time, because the shop barely makes enough for one family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the companies owe something but you don't want handouts. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A handout is something you didn't earn. If a company takes my job with a machine trained on work people like me did, paying something back isn't charity. It's settling a debt.

say: **Big tech** rushed this out without thought for **ordinary families**.
These companies **owe something**, though I'm not asking for handouts.
think: My **job is finished**, probably within a year.
A man is supposed to **provide**, and I wouldn't be.
do: Make the **wedding smaller** and keep the rest in cash.
Ask to learn the trade at his father's **repair shop**.
Live with **his parents** for a while instead of buying.
feel: **Alarmed**, and **ashamed** though he knows it isn't fair.
S2.quote: If a company takes my job with a machine trained on work people like me did, paying something back isn't charity.
fieldNote: Blames **big tech**, not government, and frames payment as a **debt owed**.
Falls back on **family**: his father's shop and his parents' home.
Feels **shame** at not being the provider, tied to his traditional values.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list and keep savings in cash
Learn electronics repair at his father's shop
Move in with his parents after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning, so families and churches and mosques should start preparing now. I'd still say the tech companies moved too fast. At work I'd keep my head down and do good work while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end with a longer fuse. I'd keep my job for maybe three years, but I know the end is coming. I'm not quick to change, so five years feels both long and short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding as planned and save hard, around 1,500 a month, but not buy the house yet. On Saturdays I'd start working at my father's repair shop to learn the trade properly. By year three or four I'd move there full time, because fixing hardware by hand buys a few years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but a slower kind. It's like knowing your car will fail its test and saving for the repair in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn the AI tools in this picture, to stay longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might use them a little near the end, if it meant another year of salary. But I wouldn't build my future on them. I'd rather build my future on something with screws and wires I can hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother Imran, who is 19 and studying computer science because he followed me. I'd tell my brother Imran to add a trade to that degree now. I'd feel responsible if Imran graduated into nothing.

say: Five years is **enough warning** for families and faith groups to prepare.
The **tech companies** still moved too fast.
think: It's the same end with a **longer fuse**.
Five years feels **both long and short** to someone slow to change.
do: Keep the **wedding** as planned but hold off on the house.
Work **Saturdays** at his father's repair shop to learn the trade.
Move to the shop **full time** by year three or four.
feel: **Alarmed**, but the slower kind, like saving for a **repair**.
S3.quote: I'd rather build my future on something with screws and wires I can hold.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the job**, only later.
Uses the time to learn his father's **repair trade** step by step.
Feels responsible for his brother **Imran**, who followed him into computing.

steps.text: Save about 1,500 a month and delay the house
Work Saturdays at his father's repair shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare themselves, so nobody should expect the state to rescue them. Families should plan together. At work I'd say the company should train its own people rather than hire new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my coding job probably lasts most of the decade, which is a long time. I'd be 37 when it ends, and I'd have a house, maybe children. It's still a worry, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house after the wedding, a modest one we could pay off quickly. I'd keep coding and save, and over the next few years I'd learn the repair trade with my father on weekends. By around 2033 I'd want to take over the shop and grow it, because hands-on repair work lasts until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can live with it. There's time to do things properly and in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2039, when robots can do hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe people would still want a person they trust to fix their things, the way they want a doctor they know. I'd be in my forties, with a paid-off house, and I'd find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything about the wedding or children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd marry next summer as planned and try for children soon after. Ten years is enough to raise a young family through. Waiting for the world to be certain means waiting forever.

say: Ten years is plenty, so nobody should expect **the state** to rescue them.
The company should **train its own people** rather than hire new ones.
think: My coding job probably lasts **most of the decade**.
It's still a worry, but I can **see a path**.
do: Buy a **modest house** after the wedding and pay it off quickly.
Learn the **repair trade** with his father on weekends.
Take over and grow the **shop** around 2033.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to live with it, with time to do things **in order**.
S4.quote: Waiting for the world to be certain means waiting forever.

His plan B is his father's **repair shop**, set for around 2033.

steps.text: Buy a modest house after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to learn anything new, and I'd start married life without a job. What would help is employers being made to pay for retraining, and proper apprenticeships, so people can earn while they learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When the work goes, people need more than money: they need a reason to get up and a community to belong to. My grandfather used to say a man without work is a man without a place, and I believe it.

headlineQuote: My grandfather used to say a man without work is a man without a place, and I believe it.
portrait: A **27-year-old** Java developer on warehouse stock software, engaged to **Amira**, a nurse.
Traditional and family-first; he wants **wedding, house, children** in that order.
Has **never used** AI tools and prefers code he can check line by line.
Calm in the plateau, **alarmed** by AGI in two or five years, anxious with ten.
His fallback is his father's **electronics repair shop**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting married life with no job and no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **apprenticeships** so people earn while they learn a trade.
